query: Which material can be used for Temperature-dependent plastic deformation behaviors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit superior temperature-dependent plastic deformation behavior compared to conventional alloys due to their inherent lattice distortions and microstructural features.
generation.material_initial_state: SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy in the as-fabricated state.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the material to a range of temperatures (from room temperature up to around 800 °C) during mechanical deformation tests.
generation.conditions: Monotonic tensile loading under controlled temperature conditions (room temperature and elevated temperatures up to ~800 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Fine grain sizes, dislocation networks, and nano-sized oxide precipitates that contribute to grain boundary and dislocation forest strengthening.
generation.mechanism: The random distribution of multiple principal elements creates lattice distortions that widen the distribution of interatomic distances, stabilizing dislocation movement and plastic deformation processes even at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The CoCrFeMnNi HEA will maintain higher yield strength and more stable plastic deformation behavior across the tested temperature range, outperforming conventional high-temperature materials.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys such as Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb gamma alloy or oxide dispersion strengthened steels, which typically show reduced yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The superior performance is expected up to approximately 800 °C; performance beyond this temperature remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences in yield strength and deformation rates at each temperature, as well as the long-term stability of the microstructural features under cyclic or prolonged high-temperature conditions, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA and conventional high-temperature alloys. Conduct systematic tensile tests at room temperature, 500 °C, 700 °C, and 800 °C. Compare yield strength, ductility, and microstructural evolution (using electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction) of the HEA to the baseline materials.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size, dislocation networks, and oxide distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not demonstrate statistically significant higher yield strength and stable plastic deformation characteristics at the elevated temperature conditions (especially at 700 °C and 800 °C) compared to the conventional alloys, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA has relatively superior mechanical properties compared to known materials manufactured with conventional manufacturing processes and additive manufacturing processes [36] – [41] , [61] , [62] . In addition, when comparing mechanical properties with EBM-built Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb gamma alloy, which is attracting great attention as a high temperature material, SLM-built HEA showed higher yield strength up to ~800 °C [69] . Furthermore, when compared to oxide dispersion strengthened steels, which are developed by cryo-milling, SLM-built HEA represented excellent high-temperature strength at temperatures greater than 700 °C [70] . In our previous study, it is confirmed that the outstanding room temperature mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA can be attributed to fine grain sizes, dislocation networks and nano-sized oxides, and based on this, the authors presented their interpretation of a multiple strengthening mechanism [33] .
